I run a landscaping crew. Rain days wreck my monthly planning — how do I forecast them instead of just hoping?

Use your own weather history as a distribution. Suppose that across the last eight Aprils, rain days in a 20-working-day month were 2, 4, 3, 6, 5, 3, 7, and 4. The mean is (2 + 4 + 3 + 6 + 5 + 3 + 7 + 4) / 8 = 34 / 8 = 4.25 rain days, so the expected workable days are 20 − 4.25 = 15.75. The median is 4 rain days. Two of the eight Aprils — 25% — had 6 or more rain days. At $1,800 of revenue per crew day, expected rain loss is 4.25 × $1,800 = $7,650 for the month.

Plan on those numbers rather than on a dry month. Schedule about 16 days of committed work, not 20, and keep a list of rain-compatible jobs — shed repairs, estimates, equipment maintenance, covered commercial sites — to fill wet days productively. Quote completion dates with the distribution in mind: 'three weeks, weather at its usual April rate' is a promise you can keep in six Aprils out of eight. And price the risk consciously: if a contract demands a fixed finish date in April, the 1-in-4 chance of a very wet month is a real cost, and it belongs in the price rather than in your margin.
I want to save $7,200. My monthly surplus varies a lot, so when will I actually get there?

Treat the surplus as a distribution and you get a date range instead of a false-precision date. Suppose in a typical month your surplus is $300 with probability 0.3, $600 with probability 0.5, and $900 with probability 0.2. The expected surplus is 0.3 × $300 + 0.5 × $600 + 0.2 × $900 = $90 + $300 + $180 = $570 a month. At that expected rate the goal takes $7,200 / $570 ≈ 12.6 months — call it about 13 months. The range matters more: if good months dominated at $900, you would arrive in $7,200 / $900 = 8 months; if lean months dominated at $300, it would take $7,200 / $300 = 24 months.

So the honest forecast is '8 to 24 months, most likely around 13' — and that range tells you what to do. If a deadline sits at month 12, you are relying on slightly-better-than-average luck, so either raise the surplus floor — the $300 months are where the plan is won — or move the deadline. Recheck every few months with your actual surpluses replacing the guessed probabilities; a forecast you update beats a precise date you defend. The goal does not change. Your knowledge of when, and of what would speed it up, does.
In our planning meeting people keep using 'forecast', 'target', and 'budget' as if they were the same number. Are they?

No — they are three different kinds of number, and confusing them corrupts all three. A forecast is your honest expectation: 'given current trends, revenue will most likely be about $240,000.' A target is an aspiration chosen to motivate and direct effort: 'we are aiming for $300,000.' A budget is an allocation decision — what you authorise spending against: 'we will spend as if $225,000 is coming in,' prudently set below the forecast so a normal shortfall does not break you. Note the gaps: the target sits $60,000 above the forecast, and the budget sits $15,000 below it, since $240,000 − $225,000 = $15,000.

Each confusion has a cost. Treat the target as the forecast and you hire and spend for $300,000 that was never expected. Treat the forecast as the budget and ordinary variance becomes a crisis. Treat the budget as a target and the team sandbags. The fix in meetings is labelling, out loud, every time: 'Is that number what we expect, what we want, or what we're spending against?' All three numbers are legitimate on the same page — as long as nobody is allowed to quietly swap one for another.
I'm a freelancer and my income swings wildly. What does a 'cone of plausible futures' look like in practice for the next year?

Draw three bands from your recent history and attach triggers to each. Suppose your last two years support: a low band of $3,200 a month, a central band of $4,800, and a high band of $6,500. Annualised, those are $3,200 × 12 = $38,400, $4,800 × 12 = $57,600, and $6,500 × 12 = $78,000. The cone is the honest statement that next year plausibly lands anywhere in that widening range — and it widens because further-out months depend on clients you have not won yet.

The bands only earn their keep with triggers. Low-band trigger: if two consecutive months land below $3,500, you cut the stated discretionary costs and start the pre-written outreach list. High-band trigger: if three consecutive months exceed $6,000, you raise rates or bank the surplus rather than upgrading fixed costs, because the high band is the least reliable of the three. Live financially on the central band, keep fixed commitments survivable on the low band, and let the high band fund irregular things — tax reserves, equipment, time off. A single 'expected income' figure would have hidden every one of those decisions.
Everyone tells me to plan to the pessimistic case. Is there a situation where that's actually the wrong advice?

Yes — when the payoff is asymmetric: the downside is capped and survivable, but the upside is large, and planning pessimistically means never taking the bet at all. Worked example. A product experiment costs $20,000 to run properly. You estimate a 0.35 probability it succeeds and returns $90,000 of profit, and a 0.65 probability it fails and the $20,000 is lost. Expected value: 0.35 × $90,000 − 0.65 × $20,000 = $31,500 − $13,000 = +$18,500. The break-even success probability is $20,000 / ($90,000 + $20,000) ≈ 0.18 — the experiment pays if it works even 18% of the time, and you believe 35%.

Planning to the pessimistic case here means assuming failure, keeping the $20,000, and forfeiting a positive-value option — repeatedly, across every experiment, which guarantees a portfolio of nothing ventured. The pessimistic case is the right plan when failure threatens survival: payroll, debt covenants, a single bet that can sink the firm. It is the wrong plan when losses are bounded, the firm can afford several attempts, and the upside compounds — early product bets, a second location test, a new service line. Often the synthesis is staging: spend a smaller sum first to buy information, then commit. The skill is not optimism or pessimism; it is matching the planning case to the shape of the payoff.
In our team meetings someone says a launch is 'likely' to succeed and everyone nods, but I suspect we all mean different things. Is that a real problem?

It is a measured problem, not a suspicion. Ask ten people to put a number on 'likely' and you will routinely get answers spread from about 55% to about 90% — one person picturing a coin-flip-plus, another picturing near-certainty, both using the same word and both leaving the meeting believing they agreed. The disagreement is invisible precisely because the word feels shared. It surfaces later, expensively: the person who meant 55% budgeted for a real chance of failure, the person who meant 90% did not, and each thinks the other was careless.

The fix is embarrassingly simple: say the number. 'Likely — I'd put it at 70%' takes two seconds longer and makes the claim checkable, arguable, and recordable. If someone resists giving a number, that itself is information: the estimate has not been thought through, and the word was covering the gap. Teams do not need to agree on the probability; they need to know which probability they are planning around. A number can be debated and later scored. A word can only be remembered differently by everyone who heard it.
I read IPCC reports and they use words like 'likely' and 'very likely'. Do those have actual definitions, or is it just scientist-speak?

They are defined terms. The IPCC publishes a calibrated language scale that ties each phrase to a probability range: 'likely' means 66–100% probability, 'very likely' means 90–100%, 'virtually certain' means 99–100%, 'about as likely as not' means 33–66%, 'unlikely' means 0–33%, and 'very unlikely' means 0–10%. When an IPCC sentence says an outcome is 'very likely,' it is making the quantitative claim that the assessed probability is at least 90% — the words are a code, and the codebook is public.

Two things follow for readers. First, translate as you read: 'likely' in an IPCC report is a stronger claim than 'likely' in a meeting, because the report's floor is 66%, not whatever the listener guesses. Second, notice the deliberate overlaps and widths — 'likely' spans 66–100% because the underlying evidence sometimes supports a floor better than a point estimate, and the scale refuses false precision. Borrowing the habit is worthwhile even if you never write about climate: if your team adopts published ranges for its words, a reader can decode you without asking. That is the entire point of calibration.
I heard intelligence analysts had this same words-and-probabilities problem decades ago. Did anyone try to fix it back then?

Yes — Sherman Kent, a senior CIA analyst, raised it in the 1950s and 1960s after finding that phrases in intelligence estimates meant wildly different things to different readers. His proposed scale attached numbers to the standard phrases: 'almost certain' ≈ 93%, 'probable' ≈ 75%, 'chances about even' ≈ 50%, 'probably not' ≈ 30%, and 'almost certainly not' ≈ 7%. Treat those as Kent's historical proposal, not as universal constants — his point was the act of fixing a scale at all.

The cautionary tale is what happened without one. Kent described an estimate calling an outcome 'probable' where the policymaker read something close to a shrug, while the analysts meant roughly three-to-one in favour — a gap he blamed for real misjudgements, and one reason he campaigned for numbers in estimates. His campaign only partly succeeded; verbal probabilities are still common in intelligence and everywhere else. The lesson travels well: if your profession's most consequential sentences carry probabilities, leaving them in uncalibrated words is not caution or style. It is an uncontrolled variable in every decision made downstream of your sentence.
My doctor said a side effect of my new medication is 'rare'. How rare is that, actually — and how should I think about it?

'Rare' is a verbal probability, and like all of them it needs translating into a frequency before you can reason with it. Ask for the natural frequency: 'Out of 1,000 people who take this, how many get it?' Suppose the answer is 1 in 1,000. In a clinic population of 10,000 patients on the drug, you would expect 10,000 / 1,000 = 10 cases; in 20,000 patients, 20 cases. That framing — actual people in an actual group — is far easier to weigh than a percentage or an adjective, and studies of risk communication consistently find doctors and patients both reason better with it.

Then put the frequency next to the benefit's frequency, in the same units: if the drug prevents a serious event in, say, 30 out of 1,000 people treated, the comparison is 30 helped versus 1 harmed per 1,000 — a judgement you can actually discuss. Also ask what 'rare' was being compared against and over what time period, since a risk per dose and a risk per year differ enormously. You are not challenging your doctor by asking; you are asking for the number their word was summarising, which is the version of the information a decision can be built on.
A report on our project says a delay is 'possible'. My boss read that as reassurance and I read it as a warning. Who's right?

Neither of you can be shown right, and that is the defect of the word. 'Possible' covers everything from a probability of 1% to 99% — it asserts only that the chance is not zero and not certain. Your boss heard 'possible but not worth worrying about'; you heard 'possible and worth preparing for'; the sentence as written supports both readings, which means it communicated almost nothing while sounding like a finding. Words like this survive in reports because they are unfalsifiable: whatever happens, the writer can say they flagged it.

Replace it with a claim someone could be wrong about. 'We estimate a 30% chance the delay occurs, based on the supplier's last three deliveries' can be debated, planned around, and scored afterwards. Even a rough range — 'somewhere between 20% and 40%' — separates a warning from a reassurance, which is the distinction your meeting actually needed. A useful house test: if a probability word could remain true under every outcome, it is decoration. Cross it out and see whether the sentence loses anything. With 'possible,' it almost never does.
I want to propose a rule for my team so our forecasts stop dissolving into vague words. What should the rule actually say?

Keep it short enough to enforce. A workable house rule: 'Every verbal probability in a decision document ships with three attachments — a number, a date, and an owner. Example format: "We estimate a 70% chance (owner: Priya, assessed 3 March) that the supplier delivers by 1 June."' Each attachment does a job. The number ends the 55%-versus-90% ambiguity that the word 'likely' carries. The date matters because probabilities expire — a 70% assessed before the supplier's factory fire is a different claim afterwards, and undated forecasts get quoted long after their assumptions die. The owner makes the forecast scoreable: someone can revisit it, learn whether their 70%s happen about 70% of the time, and get better.

Add one enforcement habit, not more rules: a monthly ten-minute review of forecasts that came due, scored without blame. Calibration improves from feedback, not from exhortation. Expect initial resistance — numbers feel exposed in a way words do not — which is precisely the evidence the rule is working. Within a quarter, the dated, owned numbers become the team's memory of what it actually believed, instead of everyone's private reconstruction of what 'likely' meant.
The forecast says there's a 'slight chance' of rain for our outdoor event. Is that an official category or just hedging?

It is closer to an official category than most people realise, though you should still ask for the number behind it. In plain-language terms used by forecast offices, wording tracks probability bands: a 'slight chance' generally corresponds to a low probability of measurable rain — roughly in the 10–20% neighbourhood — 'chance' sits higher, around 30–50%, and rain described as 'likely' means the probability is up around 60–70% or more. Treat those as literacy-level approximations, not exact thresholds: offices differ in phrasing habits, and the authoritative figure is always the numeric probability of precipitation printed with the forecast.

For your event the translation is what matters. A slight chance at, say, 20% means that in five comparable days, about one gets rained on — so the rational plan is not cancelling, and it is not ignoring the risk either; it is pricing the cheap hedge: tent on standby, a communicated wet-weather plan, programmes that survive damp. People misread 'slight chance' in both directions — as zero, because 'slight' sounds dismissive, or as a coin-flip, because any mention of rain feels alarming. Reading it as roughly one-in-five puts the decision back in proportion, which is all a probability is ever for.
People keep saying 'the expected outcome' when they seem to mean the most likely outcome. Is 'expected' being misused, or am I pedantic?

You are not pedantic — in everyday speech 'expected' means 'what I think will happen,' usually the single most likely outcome, while in forecasting expected value is a probability-weighted average that may correspond to no outcome that can actually occur. The gap matters. Take a project with three outcomes: $100,000 profit with probability 0.3, $40,000 with probability 0.5, and $0 with probability 0.2. The expected value is 0.3 × $100,000 + 0.5 × $40,000 + 0.2 × $0 = $30,000 + $20,000 + $0 = $50,000. The most likely single outcome is $40,000, at 50% — and $50,000 itself will never happen; it is not among the possible results.

Both numbers answer real questions, but different ones. The most likely outcome is what to picture when preparing for a single case. Expected value is the right basis for comparing decisions across many bets, pricing, and judging whether a repeated strategy pays — over ten such projects, results would average near $50,000 each even though no single project lands there. The misuse to watch for is quoting expected value as a prediction — 'we expect $50,000' — and then being judged against it as if it were promised. Say which one you mean: 'most likely $40,000; expected value $50,000 across many such bets.' Two clauses, and the confusion is gone.
Our review documents keep saying 'we're confident' about delivery dates. A colleague says that phrase is doing something sneaky. What do they mean?

'We're confident' smuggles a probability claim past the scrutiny a number would receive. If a document said 'we estimate an 85% chance of delivering by June,' reviewers would ask the obvious questions: based on what, what fills the other 15%, who owns the estimate? 'We're confident' asserts roughly the same thing while presenting itself as a mood rather than a claim — there is nothing visible to challenge, no basis to request, and no way to score it afterwards. It also scales invisibly: one writer's 'confident' means 60%, another's means 95%, and the document reads identically either way.

The arithmetic of scoring shows what is lost. If a team makes 20 forecasts at a genuine 90% confidence, about 20 × 0.10 = 2 of them should fail — a well-calibrated team expects and budgets for roughly two misses. A team that merely says 'confident' twenty times and misses six has no mechanism to notice it was really operating near 70%, because the claims were never pinned down. The fix is not banning the word; it is refusing to let it travel alone. 'We're confident — about 80%, because the two longest tasks are already done' can be reviewed, planned around, and learned from. Confidence that cannot state its number has not earned the authority the word borrows.
Can you show me the same forecast written three ways — vague, with calibrated words, and with a number — and what each version costs the reader?

Take one claim: a supplier delivery arriving by 1 June. Vague version: 'Delivery by June is possible, and we're fairly optimistic.' Cost to the reader: total. 'Possible' spans 1% to 99%, 'fairly optimistic' adds tone without information, and the reader must either guess a probability — each reader guessing differently — or plan for everything, which means planning for nothing. The writer, meanwhile, can never be wrong, which is why such sentences survive.

Verbal-calibrated version, using a published scale such as the IPCC's: 'Delivery by 1 June is likely.' A reader who knows the codebook decodes 'likely' as 66–100% — a real improvement, narrowing the range and making the claim comparable across documents. The cost: the reader must know and trust the scale, and the range is still wide enough to hide the difference between two-in-three and near-certain. Numeric version: 'We estimate a 75% chance of delivery by 1 June, assessed 3 March.' The cost moves to the writer, who must commit, show a date, and accept being scored — and the reader gains everything: they can plan to the 25% failure case, compare this claim against other teams', and later check whether the forecaster's 75%s land about three times in four. Each step transfers effort from reader to writer. Good forecasting writing accepts that transfer deliberately.
Our board deck says 'revenue will probably grow next year.' My CFO says that sentence is useless. What is she objecting to, and what should the sentence say instead?

She is objecting that the sentence cannot be checked, argued with, or planned around. 'Probably' has no number: studies of verbal probability phrases consistently find that different readers map the same word to very different percentages, so one director hears 55% and another hears 90%. 'Grow' has no size: 0.3% growth and 30% growth both satisfy it. And 'next year' has no test date or comparison point.

An honest version carries four parts — a number, an interval, a date, and a definition. For example: 'We estimate a 70% chance that full-year 2027 revenue exceeds the 2026 figure of $4.2M, and a 50% chance it lands between $4.5M and $5.1M.' Now the claim can be wrong in a useful way: in January 2028 you can open the deck, compare, and learn whether your forecasting process is calibrated. The interval also does planning work the adjective cannot — the low end sizes the cash buffer you need, the high end sizes the capacity you might want. A forecast you cannot score later is not a forecast; it is a mood with a slide behind it.

In our house, 'it'll probably rain' means totally different things depending on who says it. My partner packs an umbrella at the slightest hint; I only say 'probably' when I'm nearly sure. How do we fix this without being weird about it?

You are not disagreeing about the weather — you are using the same word for different numbers, and the fix is a short calibration conversation, not an argument. Try this: each of you privately writes down what percentage you mean by your usual phrases — 'might rain,' 'probably rain,' 'almost certainly rain.' Households routinely discover spreads like 30% versus 80% hiding inside one shared word, which explains years of 'you said it would rain!' friction.

Then agree on a household convention. A simple one: 'probably' means more likely than not, above 50%; 'likely' means around 70% or more; 'almost certain' means 90%+. Or skip words for the decisions that matter and use the forecast's own number: most weather apps give a percentage, so 'the app says 40%' ends the translation problem entirely. The umbrella question is separate, and worth separating: whether to carry one depends on the cost of getting wet, not just the probability. At 30% rain, a person with a laptop bag and a long walk should pack one; a person popping to the car should not. Same forecast, different stakes, both rational.

We're deciding whether to launch a product nationally. Historically about 30% of launches like ours succeed. Our test market just came back strong. How much should that actually move our confidence? I don't want vibes, I want the arithmetic.

Use frequencies — they make the update impossible to fudge. Start with 100 launches similar to yours: 30 succeed and 70 fail, which is your 30% base rate before the test.

Now add what a strong test market means in that reference class: suppose a strong result shows up in 24 of the 30 successes, but also in 14 of the 70 failures — strong tests are encouraging, not decisive, because some doomed products test well. You have now observed a strong test, so your product is in the group of launches with strong tests: 24 successes + 14 failures = 38 launches. The chance of success given the strong test is 24 / (24 + 14) = 24/38 ≈ 63%.

So the honest update is 30% → about 63%: the test roughly doubled your confidence, and that is a big, decision-relevant move — but it is not the 90%+ certainty a triumphant test-market presentation usually implies. The 14 false positives in the denominator are the whole lesson. Before you commit, the most valuable next question is what drives those 14: if strong tests in your category often reflect novelty effects that fade, your 63% is generous; if they fade rarely, it may be conservative. Either way, argue about the frequencies, not the adjectives.

Our vibration sensor flags equipment faults on a production line. Faults are rare, the sensor is '95% accurate' according to the vendor, and my team wants to shut the line down at every alarm. Walk me through what an alarm actually means, in frequencies.

Work with 1,000 machines (or machine-days) so every percentage becomes a count you can point at. Say faults are genuinely rare: 20 of the 1,000 are actually faulty, a 2% base rate. Take the vendor's accuracy claim in its most useful form: the sensor catches 18 of the 20 real faults — it misses 2. Now the number vendors quote less loudly, the false-alarm rate: suppose it flags 98 of the 980 healthy machines, about 10%.

Total alarms: 18 real + 98 false = 116. So when the alarm sounds, the chance the machine is actually faulty is 18 / 116 ≈ 15.5%. Roughly 5 of every 6 alarms are false — not because the sensor is bad, but because healthy machines outnumber faulty ones 49 to 1, so even a modest false-alarm rate floods the alarm pool.

That arithmetic argues against shutting the line at every alarm and for a two-stage response: an alarm triggers a cheap, fast inspection (which is itself a second test that updates the probability again), and only an alarm plus a failed inspection stops the line. It also tells you what to negotiate with the vendor: cutting the false-alarm rate from 10% to 5% would nearly double the alarm's meaning — 18 / (18 + 49) ≈ 27% — while pushing detection from 18 to 19 of 20 barely moves it. With rare events, specificity is where the value is.

A pundit predicted in the preseason that our team would win the division. It's week 12, the team is 3-8, the quarterback is injured, and he still says 'I stand by my prediction.' What exactly is wrong with that, beyond stubbornness?

The prediction he made in the preseason was a claim about the world as it looked then: a healthy roster, a full schedule ahead, every outcome still possible. Twelve weeks of games are new evidence — eight losses, an injured quarterback, rivals' records — and a probability that refuses to move when the world changes is no longer describing the world. It is describing his ego.

There is also a quiet bait-and-switch in 'I stand by it.' In the preseason, 'they'll win the division' presumably meant something like 'this is the most likely outcome' or 'I'd put it above 50%.' By week 12, with the team needing to win out and get help, the honest probability might be in the low single digits. Defending the sentence while its meaning collapses lets him claim vindication on a technicality if a miracle happens, and shrug 'nobody's perfect' if it doesn't. A forecaster who never updates can never really be wrong, which is exactly why his predictions carry no information. The respectable version sounds like: 'My preseason case rested on the quarterback staying healthy. That assumption is gone, so my number moves from about 55% to under 10%.' Updating is not flip-flopping; refusing to update is the actual failure.

I'm the opposite problem: I revise my project-completion forecast after every standup. One blocked ticket and I push the date a week; one good day and I pull it back. My team says my forecasts are useless. Are they right?

Mostly, yes — and the reason is subtle: your forecast now has so much variance of its own that it adds noise instead of removing it. A completion estimate is supposed to average over the ordinary wobbles of a project — the blocked ticket, the sick day, the surprisingly easy task — because over a multi-week project those wobbles roughly cancel. When you re-forecast after each one, you are treating daily noise as if it were a permanent change in the project's speed, so your date swings by weeks in response to events that move the true expected date by hours.

Think of it as two questions. Has something changed that affects all remaining work — a lost team member, a cut feature, a newly discovered dependency? Then update, immediately and by a lot. Or has something merely happened — one bad day inside a distribution of bad and good days you already knew about? Then the correct update is zero, because that event was already priced into your interval. A useful discipline: keep an anchor forecast with an interval, and only revise it on a fixed cadence or when a structural fact changes — and when you do revise, write down which structural fact caused it. If you cannot name one, you are chasing wobble. Your team will trust a forecast that moves rarely and explains itself over one that moves daily and explains nothing.

Hurricane forecasts seem to get dramatically better in the last two days before landfall. What new information actually arrives to narrow the cone, or is it just that there's less time left to be wrong in?

Both, and it is worth separating them because only one of them is skill. Part of the narrowing is mechanical: a forecast for 24 hours from now spans less possible wandering than a forecast for 120 hours from now, simply because the storm has fewer hours in which to deviate. Even a forecaster who learned nothing new would see the cone shrink as landfall approaches.

But real information does arrive, and it is specific. Aircraft reconnaissance flies into the storm and measures its actual center, pressure, and wind structure, replacing satellite estimates with observations — the model's starting picture of the present gets sharper. The steering currents that push the storm — the ridge and trough patterns in the upper atmosphere — become clearer as the atmosphere itself evolves into the configuration that will do the steering, and as weather balloons and satellites sample it. Forecasters also watch the spread among many model runs: when independent models converge on similar tracks, confidence genuinely rises; when they diverge, an honest cone stays wide.

Two cautions. The cone describes uncertainty in the track of the center, based on past errors — it is not a boundary of danger, and impacts routinely occur outside it. And a narrowing cone late in the game should not be read backwards as 'the early forecast was bad.' The early wide cone was the honest statement of what was knowable then.
I started keeping a diary of my own predictions. For the twenty events where I said '80% confident,' only 13 actually happened. What does that tell me, precisely, and how do I fix it?

It tells you your 80% is not an 80%. If your confidence were calibrated, then out of 20 events you called 80%, about 16 should have happened — 0.80 × 20 = 16. You got 13, which is 65%. So the events you label '80% confident' behave, in your track record, more like 65% events. That gap has a name: overconfidence — your stated probabilities sit systematically higher than your hit rate.

Twenty events is a small sample, so don't over-correct on this batch alone — chance alone could produce 13 from a true 80% process occasionally. But treat it as evidence, especially if your other confidence levels show the same pattern (your '90%'s landing 75% of the time, say). The practical fixes are two. First, shade toward the base rate: before settling on a number, ask how often this kind of thing happens in general, and start there rather than at your gut's enthusiasm. Second, widen your language: when your diary says your felt-80% performs like 65%, then say 65% until your record earns the higher number back. Keep the diary going — calibration is one of the few forecasting skills that measurably improves just from scoring yourself, because the feedback is unambiguous and impossible to argue with.

Show me how a sales pipeline forecast should actually update week to week. Our stages have stated probabilities and I want to see the expected value recomputed as deals move, not just a new gut-feel total.

Set it up once, then let arithmetic do the updating. Week 1, three deals with stage probabilities: Deal A, $100,000 at 60% (late negotiation) contributes 100,000 × 0.60 = $60,000. Deal B, $50,000 at 30% contributes $15,000. Deal C, $200,000 at 10% (early stage) contributes $20,000. Expected pipeline value: 60,000 + 15,000 + 20,000 = $95,000. That number, not the $350,000 headline sum, is the forecast.

Week 2, the facts change: A advances to 80% after a signed term sheet: $80,000. B is lost — gone entirely, $0, and it leaves the pipeline rather than lingering at a hopeful 5%. C advances to 25% after a technical review: 200,000 × 0.25 = $50,000. A new deal D enters at $80,000 and 20%: $16,000. New expected value: 80,000 + 0 + 50,000 + 16,000 = $146,000 — up $51,000, about 54% on the week.

Notice what made the number move: stage changes and an exit, each with a stated reason — not anyone's optimism level. Two disciplines keep this honest. Use the same stage probabilities every week (if 'technical review passed' is 25%, it is 25% for every deal, not 40% for the rep's favorite), and when a deal's stage changes, log why. Then, quarterly, check calibration: of all deals that sat at 30%, did roughly 30% close? If only 15% did, your stage probabilities — not your reps — are the first thing to fix.
My forecast intervals get narrower as I collect more data, but how much narrower, exactly? I keep hearing 'it shrinks with the square root of n' and I want to see it in numbers.

Here it is concretely. Suppose you're estimating an average — say, average delivery time — and the individual observations vary with a standard deviation of 100 (minutes, dollars, whatever your units are). The standard error of your average is 100 / √n, and a roughly 95% interval is your estimate ± 1.96 standard errors.

With n = 25: standard error = 100 / 5 = 20, so the interval half-width is 1.96 × 20 = 39.2. With n = 100: standard error = 100 / 10 = 10, half-width 19.6. With n = 400: standard error = 100 / 20 = 5, half-width 9.8. Read the pattern off the numbers: quadrupling the data halves the interval. Going from 25 to 100 observations bought you a 2× improvement; getting another 2× costs you 400 total, and the next 2× would cost 1,600.

This is the arithmetic behind a common disappointment: the first batch of data shrinks uncertainty dramatically, and later batches feel like they barely help — they are helping exactly as much as the square-root law says, which is less and less per observation. Two caveats before you apply it. This assumes the new data is drawn from the same process as the old; 400 observations of last year's market narrow your interval around last year's truth. And it assumes independent observations — if your 400 data points are really 40 customers measured 10 times each, your effective n is much closer to 40, and your honest interval is much wider than 9.8.

A colleague is trying to convince me our product caused a client's sudden sales spike — he has one dramatic story about the week they installed it. I have boring data on a thousand clients. How do I explain why my table beats his story?

His story answers the question 'can you picture it happening?' and your table answers 'how often does it happen?' — and only the second one supports a decision. A single vivid case has no denominator. Sales spikes happen for dozens of reasons — seasonality, a competitor's stockout, a mention somewhere, plain randomness — and a spike was guaranteed to happen to somebody in a thousand-client base this quarter. Your colleague then found the spike and worked backwards to a cause, which means the story was selected because it was dramatic, not because it was representative.

Your table fixes the selection problem by counting everyone: how many of the 1,000 clients spiked in a given period, split by whether they had installed the product, and how that compares with the base rate of spikes before anyone installed anything. If installers and non-installers spike at similar rates, the product explanation is dead no matter how good the story is. If installers spike at, say, double the rate, you have something real — and even then the table, not the anecdote, tells you the size of the effect.

Be kind about it, because the pull of the story is human, not stupid: a narrative with a named client and a timeline feels like evidence in a way a rate never will. The discipline is to let stories generate hypotheses and let tables test them. The moment a story is asked to carry the weight of a rate, it breaks.
Sometimes I get a new signal and I'm not sure it should change my forecast at all. How do I tell whether a piece of evidence is actually informative before I update on it?

Ask one question: does this signal show up at different rates when the thing happens versus when it doesn't? If the rates are nearly equal, the signal is nearly worthless, and the honest update is nearly zero — no matter how official or expensive the signal looks.

Work it in frequencies. Take 1,000 past cases where your prior was 40%: 400 succeeded, 600 failed. Your new indicator — say, a particular pattern in early usage — appeared in 51% of the successes, that's 204 cases, and in 49% of the failures, that's 294 cases. Now you observe the indicator on a new case. It sits in the pool of 204 + 294 = 498 cases with the indicator, of which 204 succeeded: 204 / 498 ≈ 41%. Your forecast moves from 40% to about 41%. The likelihood ratio here is 51/49 ≈ 1.04, essentially 1, and a likelihood ratio of 1 means the evidence carries no information at all — the posterior equals the prior by construction.

Contrast that with an indicator appearing in 80% of successes and 20% of failures — a likelihood ratio of 4 — which would move the same 40% prior dramatically. The habit to build: before updating, demand the two rates. Anyone presenting a signal should be able to say how often it fires in both worlds. If they only know how often it fires in the world they want — 'most winners had this pattern!' — you are missing the denominator that decides whether to move at all.
Should I update my forecasts whenever news arrives, or on a fixed schedule? My team argues about this every planning cycle.

Mostly on a schedule, with an exception for genuinely structural news — and the reason is what each style does to your decision-making. Updating on news sounds responsive, but news arrives unevenly, is selected for drama, and reaches you precisely when emotions run hottest. Teams that update on headlines end up re-litigating the plan weekly, overweighting whatever happened most recently, and quietly moving goalposts so often that no forecast is ever scored — there is always a newer one.

A fixed cadence — say, a monthly forecast review — batches the news. By review day, some alarming stories have resolved themselves, some quiet developments have compounded, and you can weigh a month of evidence at once instead of reacting to each item at peak vividness. It also creates a clean record: the forecast as of each date, scored later, which is how calibration improves.

The exception: some events change the structure of the problem itself — a regulation lands, a key supplier dies, a competitor exits. Waiting for the monthly review to acknowledge those is not discipline, it is denial. The rule that separates the two: update off-schedule when a fact changes what is possible or what things cost, not when a fact changes how you feel about the quarter. If you cannot state the structural change in one sentence, it can wait for the schedule.

Two analysts on my team looked at the same test results for the same product and came back with very different probabilities of success — about 31% and 80%. One of them must be doing the math wrong, right?

Not necessarily — and working it in frequencies shows exactly where the difference lives. Give both analysts the same evidence: a test signal that appears in 80% of products that go on to succeed and in 20% of products that fail. Now give them different, explicitly stated starting points based on different reference classes.

Analyst One works on experimental products, where the historical success rate is 10%. Out of 1,000 such products: 100 succeed, 900 fail. The signal appears in 80 of the 100 successes and in 180 of the 900 failures. After seeing the signal: 80 / (80 + 180) = 80/260 ≈ 31%. Analyst Two works on line extensions, where the historical success rate is 50%. Out of 1,000: 500 succeed, 500 fail. The signal appears in 400 successes and 100 failures. After the same signal: 400 / (400 + 100) = 400/500 = 80%. Both calculations are correct. Identical evidence, different priors, different posteriors — that is not a bug in the method; it is the method honestly reporting that the evidence, while strong, is not strong enough to erase a real difference in starting points.

So the argument to have is not about arithmetic but about the prior: which reference class does this product actually belong to — experimental launches or line extensions? That is a substantive, checkable question about your company's history. Insist that priors be stated before results arrive, in writing. A forecaster who names a prior can be argued with and can learn; one who hides it inside a conclusion cannot. And note the honest implication: if you want the two analysts to converge, you don't need more debate — you need either agreement on the reference class or a stronger test whose signal rates differ enough to swamp the prior gap.
After the hurricane, the mayor said 'the forecast was wrong — we weren't even in the cone, and we got flooded.' The meteorologists say the forecast verified. Who's right?

Both are describing different things, and the gap between them is the failure. The cone is a statement about the track of the storm's center: historically, the center stays inside the cone about two-thirds of the time, and the cone's size comes from past forecast errors. If the center passed outside the mayor's city but within the cone's track uncertainty, the track forecast may indeed have verified as designed.

But nobody experiences a storm's center. They experience wind, rain, and surge, and those extend far beyond the center — surge especially is driven by the storm's size, its angle of approach, and the coastline's shape, and destructive water can arrive well outside the cone, sometimes on the side of the storm farthest from the landfall point. A city outside the cone can flood catastrophically in a perfectly 'correct' forecast.

So the meteorologists are right about the quantity they forecast, and the mayor is right that the communication failed him: if a reasonable official reads the graphic as 'outside the cone means safe,' the graphic — not the reader — has the problem. The fix that forecasters have been moving toward is impact-based messaging alongside the cone: separate, explicit statements about surge, rainfall, and wind for specific places, stated in their own right rather than inferred from a track line. Judge a forecast by whether the decisions made from it were good, not only by whether the line verified.

I audited a forecaster who gives '90% confidence intervals.' Over his last 20 forecasts, the actual outcome landed inside his interval only 14 times. He says that's 'close enough given randomness.' Is it?

No — the audit caught a real defect, and the numbers show it. A 90% interval is a promise about coverage: over many forecasts, about 90% of outcomes should land inside. Over 20 forecasts, that is an expectation of about 18 hits — 0.90 × 20 = 18. He delivered 14, which is 70% coverage. His so-called 90% intervals are behaving like 70% intervals.

Could randomness alone explain a 14 when you expect 18? Occasionally, yes — 20 is a small sample, and even a perfectly calibrated forecaster will have unlucky stretches. But 'could be luck' is not 'close enough': the shortfall is the single most likely sign that his intervals are systematically too narrow, which is the most common failure in all of forecasting. Research on expert judgment repeatedly finds intervals capturing far fewer outcomes than their stated confidence — overconfidence is the default, not the exception.

The professional response is not to defend the label but to repair the instrument: widen the intervals until audited coverage matches the claim, then re-audit. If he wants to keep the intervals he has, the honest move is to relabel them — sell them as 70% intervals, which is what they demonstrably are. A forecaster's credibility should rest on the match between what he claims and what his record shows, and right now his record is the more truthful of the two.
Following up on that audit: his intervals are capturing 70% when he claims 90%. Roughly how much wider do they need to be? I want the reasoning, not just 'widen them.'

There is a principled back-of-envelope, with a caveat at the end. Suppose his forecast errors are roughly bell-shaped and his intervals are symmetric — estimate ± some multiple of the error spread. A true 90% interval needs to reach about ±1.645 standard deviations of the error distribution. An interval that actually captures 70% is reaching only about ±1.036 standard deviations. The ratio tells you the correction: 1.645 / 1.036 ≈ 1.59. So as a first repair, his half-widths need to grow by a factor of roughly 1.6 — an interval of ±10 becomes about ±16 — if the shape of his errors stays the same and only the width was wrong.

Now the caveats, which matter as much as the factor. First, this assumes his misses are a scaling problem. Audit the misses themselves: if several outcomes landed far outside — not just past the edge but nowhere near it — his error distribution has fatter tails than the bell curve, and multiplying by 1.6 will still leave the extremes uncovered; he needs wider intervals and a different mental model of the extremes. Second, 20 forecasts is a thin audit, so treat 1.6 as a starting correction, not a constant of nature: apply it, keep forecasting, and re-audit after the next 20. If coverage climbs to 17 or 18 of 20, the repair worked. The general principle travels well beyond this case: let measured coverage, not confidence, set the width — and re-measure, because the first fix is usually an underestimate.
Our analytics team forecasts next month's ad clicks to three decimal places. Impressive, right? Our actual decision is how much revenue to budget for. Something feels off but I can't name it.

You can name it now: they are being precise about the wrong variable. Clicks are not the decision. Revenue is — and revenue depends on clicks multiplied by conversion rate multiplied by order value, each of which carries its own uncertainty. A click forecast of, say, 1,248,392.617 (the decimals alone should make you suspicious — no process on earth knows clicks to the nearest thousandth) tells you almost nothing about the revenue range, because modest uncertainty in conversion rate and order value swamps the false precision in clicks. The budget decision needs a revenue interval; what it got was a very exact answer to a question nobody was asking.

This failure is attractive because the wrong variable is usually the measurable one. Clicks arrive daily, cleanly counted; revenue attribution is messy and delayed. So the team optimizes the forecast it can make look rigorous. The tell is the decimal places: precision in a forecast should never exceed the precision of the least certain link in the chain that connects it to the decision. The fix is to forecast the decision variable directly, with an interval that honestly compounds the uncertainties along the chain — clicks ± some range, times conversion ± some range, times order value ± some range. The resulting revenue interval will look embarrassingly wide next to the three-decimal click number. It will also be the first forecast in the chain that could actually change a budget decision, which is the entire point.

A startup showed me a chart: their user numbers for years 1–5 were 10, 13, 16, 19, 22 thousand, a beautiful straight line, and they extended it to year 20 to justify their valuation. What's wrong with the picture?

Extend their own line and watch it indict itself. The values rise by exactly 3 thousand a year, so the fitted rule is users = 7 + 3 × year (in thousands). Year 10 gives 7 + 30 = 37 thousand. Year 20 gives 7 + 60 = 67 thousand. Now ask the question the chart avoids: 67 thousand out of what? If their total addressable market is, say, 60 thousand users, the line has them capturing more than the entire market — 67 > 60 — and it keeps going: year 30 implies 97 thousand, year 100 implies 307 thousand, in a market of 60. A straight line fitted to early growth contains no mechanism for saturation, competition, or churn, so extended far enough it always predicts the impossible. The only question is how far out the absurdity starts.

Notice also how little data the line rests on: five points, all from the easiest growth phase, when the earliest, most enthusiastic users arrive and the market is nowhere near tapped. Early growth in almost every real process is the worst guide to late growth, because the forces that eventually bend the curve — running out of easy customers, competitors reacting, the product hitting its natural niche size — have not switched on yet during years 1–5, so the data contains no trace of them. The honest version of their chart shows the line stopping near the data, an interval that fans out rapidly beyond it, and an explicit saturation story: what the ceiling is and why. A trend is a description of the past. The moment it is extended past the data's edge, it becomes a claim about mechanisms — and it should be forced to argue like one.

Our town's flood plan uses flood-frequency tables built from river data collected in the 1990s. An engineer told me 'the base rate changed.' What does she mean, and does it really invalidate the old tables?

She means the river the tables describe may no longer be the river you have. A flood-frequency table is a base rate: 'a flood of this size occurred, historically, about once every N years.' That statement silently assumes the process generating floods is stationary — same watershed, same rainfall patterns, same land use. Change the watershed and the same table stops describing your town even though every number in it was honestly measured.

The changes are concrete, not hypothetical hand-waving: upstream development replaces absorbent ground with pavement, so the same rain delivers more water to the river faster; channels get dredged, leveed, or built around; and rainfall patterns themselves can shift over decades. Each of these moves the true frequency of a given flood size, generally toward 'more often than the old table says' in a developing watershed — though the direction and size of the shift are local questions, not universal ones, which is exactly why she is flagging it rather than handing you a correction factor.

The old tables are not worthless — they are a measurement of a past regime, and often the only long record available. The failure would be using them as if the regime were guaranteed. The careful approach treats the historical frequencies as one input, asks what has physically changed in the watershed since, and stress-tests the plan against floods somewhat more frequent than the table claims. When a base rate comes from a world that has been rebuilt, quoting it to the decimal is false confidence in its purest form.

Something odd happened at my company: leadership turned our sales forecast into the sales team's official target, and suddenly the forecasts started coming true — on paper. Deals get booked in weird ways near quarter-end now. What happened?

The forecast stopped measuring the business and started steering it — and a measure people are rewarded for hitting stops being a measure. This is the pattern often summarized as Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Your forecast was originally an estimate of what would happen. The moment it became the number the team is judged against, every incentive flipped: instead of reporting the future honestly, the team now manufactures agreement with the prediction.

The quarter-end weirdness is the signature. Deals get pulled forward from next quarter, booked early, split, or recorded with generous interpretations of 'closed' — each one individually defensible, collectively a corruption of the data. And here is the deeper damage: your forecasting process now feeds on the gamed numbers. Next year's 'actuals,' the base rates, the stage probabilities — all of it is contaminated by behavior that was aimed at the metric rather than the customer, so even a future honest forecaster inherits poisoned history.

The structural fix is separation: forecasts and targets should be different numbers owned by different processes. A target is allowed to be aspirational — it is a management tool. A forecast must be allowed to disappoint — it is an information tool. When the same number has to do both jobs, it ends up doing the first and faking the second, and leadership ends up steering by an instrument the crew is quietly bending toward whatever reading gets them home.

Our annual planning document leads with: 'Revenue next year will be $12.4M.' One number, no range, stated like a fact. Rewrite that headline the way an honest forecaster would, and explain what changed.

An honest version might read: 'Our central estimate for next year's revenue is $12.4M. We put roughly a 50% chance on landing between $11.2M and $13.1M, and a 90% chance on landing between $9.8M and $14.6M. The low end assumes the delayed product launch slips another quarter; the high end assumes it ships on time and the new channel performs at the level of its first-quarter test.'

Three things changed. First, the point estimate survived — honesty does not mean refusing to commit to a number — but it was demoted from 'the future' to 'the center of a distribution,' which is all a point estimate ever is. Second, the intervals carry the planning value: the 90% low end, $9.8M, is the number the cash plan should survive; the spread between $11.2M and $13.1M tells hiring how much uncertainty it is really absorbing. A single $12.4M forces every downstream plan to pretend the same false certainty, so the whole company ends up brittle in exactly the same place. Third, the scenarios name the drivers. Now a reader can argue productively — 'I think the launch risk is bigger than that' — instead of arguing about a bare number nobody can decompose. A headline that cannot be disagreed with in parts cannot be improved, and a plan built on it cannot be stress-tested. The rewrite is longer. That length is the honesty.
A famous investor's book quotes his five most brilliant market calls. A friend says this proves he's a great forecaster. I suspect a trick. What is it?

The trick is that you are seeing the numerator without the denominator. Five brilliant calls prove almost nothing until you know how many calls he made in total. If he made six predictions and five were brilliant, that is a remarkable record. If he made two hundred and the book prints the five that worked, you are looking at the expected yield of chance plus an editor. Any active forecaster who opines constantly will accumulate a handful of spectacular hits by luck alone — the question is always what the misses cost and whether the hits beat the base rate of the predictions he was making.

This is survivorship in its purest form: the track record that reaches you has been filtered by the outcome. The failed calls are not quoted, the abandoned newsletters are not reprinted, and the forecasters whose five best calls were still mediocre are not offered book deals at all — so the population of 'proven forecasters' you can name is itself a survivor pool. Even the man's own memory cooperates: people genuinely remember their reasoning on the winners more vividly than on the losers.

The test to demand is boring and decisive: a complete, timestamped record — every call, made in advance, scored by a rule set in advance. Forecasters who are actually good tend to welcome this, because their edge survives full accounting. Forecasters whose reputations depend on the highlight reel will explain, at length, why their art cannot be reduced to mere scoring. That explanation is itself data.
After our supply chain collapsed during a freak disruption, our risk manager said 'nobody could have foreseen this — it was a black swan.' How do I tell whether that's true or just an excuse?

Ask him to complete one sentence: 'Our risk model covered the following scenarios, and this event fell outside them because…' A genuine black swan survives that question; an excuse collapses under it. There are three possibilities, and they have very different owners. First: the event was inside the model's stated scope and the model assigned it a probability that was simply low — then it was foreseen, priced as unlikely, and the outcome is bad luck, not a black swan; a 5% event happening is the 5% world arriving on schedule. Second: the event was outside the stated scope — the model covered supplier bankruptcies, say, but explicitly not port closures — then the model may be blameless, but the scope decision is not: someone chose what the model was allowed to see, and the honest conversation is about whether that choice was defensible with what was known. Third: there was no stated scope at all — no written list of what the risk process did and did not cover. That is the most common case, and in it 'black swan' is unfalsifiable, because a model that never said what it excluded can claim every failure was excluded.

The phrase also does quiet rhetorical work: it converts a question about preparation into a fact about the universe. Push past it to the practical question — regardless of foreseeability, was the exposure survivable? A supply chain that collapses when any single unlikely thing happens was fragile to the whole category of surprises, including the ones still unnamed. You cannot forecast every shock. You can refuse to build a system that one shock of any kind destroys — and that refusal does not require seeing the future at all.

A risk report at my firm treats a '5-sigma loss day' as essentially impossible — once in the age of the universe stuff. But our own data table shows days that extreme turning up regularly. Do the math for me: how impossible are they supposed to be, and how does reality compare?

Run both numbers side by side. Under a normal (bell-curve) model, a move beyond 5 standard deviations — counting both tails — has probability about 5.7 × 10⁻⁷, roughly 0.000057%. As a waiting time, that is about 1 day in 1.74 million: at 250 trading days a year, you would expect one such day every seven thousand years or so. 'Essentially impossible' is, under that model, a fair summary.

Now your firm's own table: suppose it records 40 such days in 10,000 trading days — about 40 years of data. That is an observed frequency of 40 / 10,000 = 0.004, or 0.4% — about 1 day in 250, roughly one a year. Compare the two: 0.004 versus 0.00000057. Reality is delivering the event on the order of 7,000 times more often than the normal model promises. That is not a small calibration error; it is the model describing a different universe.

The reason has a name: fat tails. Financial returns — and many natural and operational quantities — produce extreme values far more often than the bell curve allows, because the underlying process is not the sum of many small independent nudges: volatility clusters, correlations spike in a crisis, and one big move triggers others. The practical consequence is that any interval or capital buffer built from the normal model understates the extremes while looking perfectly reasonable in the middle, where it fits well. The fix is not a fancier slogan but different arithmetic: estimate tail frequencies from the historical record itself, or use distributions with explicitly fat tails, and size your buffers for the 1-in-250 day your own table shows — not the 1-in-1.74-million day your model imagines.
